INTRODUCTION SECTION

Descriptive and inferential statistics are very important in modern data analysis and decision-making. Descriptive statistics allow researchers to organize, summarize, and present data in an understandable format, while inferential statistics help draw conclusions about a bigger population based on sample data (Bluman, 2017). These statistical techniques are fundamental for interpreting market performance and making informed strategic decisions.

Companies often experience different levels of success across various regions. Some areas may have high sales, while others might struggle due to factors like poor infrastructure or low demand. Understanding these differences is important for business strategy.

The dataset under research contains market performance metrics, including sales, profits, shipping costs, and product categories across different geographical regions. This study implements modern data analysis techniques using R to extract valuable insights from this dataset. The approach includes descriptive statistical analysis, comparative assessments across regions, and data visualization techniques such as boxplots, histograms, and bar charts. The findings will support strategic decisions related to market expansion, product distribution, and operational efficiency (Thompson, 2023; Wilson, 2022; Roberts, 2023).

The dataset contains sales, profits, shipping costs, and product categories across global regions, providing insights into market dynamics. Using R, this data can be analyzed to identify trends, compare regional performance, and optimize strategies. R’s robust tools for visualization and statistical modeling make it invaluable for extracting actionable insights (Roberts, 2022).

To address the problem, I will use R for data analysis, descriptive statistics to summarize market performance and inferential statistics to identify trends. Visualization tools such as boxplots, histograms, and bar charts will help illustrate regional disparities, while statistical summaries will support data-driven decision-making.

Task 2: Market Categories and Frequencies
Description of task: This task analyzes the distribution of different market categories in our dataset. Understanding the frequency of each market category helps us identify the main markets represented in our data and their relative importance. 

market_freq <- M2Data %>%
  count(Market, name = "Frequency") %>%
  arrange(desc(Frequency))

kable(market_freq, 
      caption = "Market Categories and Their Frequencies",
      col.names = c("Market Category", "Frequency")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = FALSE)
Market Categories and Their Frequencies
Market Category Frequency
Asia Pacific 365
Europe 248
USCA 200
LATAM 133
Africa 54


Observations: The market analysis reveals five distinct geographical regions, with Asia Pacific dominating at 365 occurrences, followed by Europe (248) and USCA (200). This distribution shows a clear concentration in Asian and European markets, which together represent nearly 61% of all entries. The notably smaller presence in Africa (54 occurrences) suggests potential untapped opportunities or market development needs in this region.



Task 3: Bar Graph of Market Categories and Frequencies
Description of task: This task visualizes the market distribution using a horizontal bar graph, which provides a clear visual representation of the frequency distribution across different markets. The graph includes frequency values and uses distinct colors for better visualization. 

market_freq <- M2Data %>%
  count(Market) %>%
  arrange(n)  

par(mar = c(5, 8, 4, 2))  
barplot_data <- barplot(market_freq$n,
        names.arg = market_freq$Market,
        horiz = TRUE,
        col = brewer.pal(n = nrow(market_freq), name = "Set3"),
        las = 1, 
        xlim = c(0, max(market_freq$n) * 1.2),  
        main = "Market Distribution",
        xlab = "Frequency")

text(x = market_freq$n,
     y = barplot_data,
     labels = market_freq$n,
     pos = 4,
     cex = 0.8)


Observations: The horizontal bar graph provides a clear visual representation of market frequencies. Each market is represented by a distinct color for easy differentiation. The actual frequency values are displayed at the end of each bar for precise interpretation. Asia Pacific leads with 365 occurrences, followed by Europe (248) and USCA (200), showing a strong presence in developed markets.


Task 4: Pie Chart of Product Categories in Africa
Description of task: This task focuses on analyzing the distribution of product categories specifically in the African market. So by filtering the data for Africa and then will create a pie chart to visualize the product category distribution within this market. 

colnames(M2Data)
##  [1] "Region"              "Market"              "Company_Segment"    
##  [4] "Product_Category"    "Product_SubCategory" "Price"              
##  [7] "Quantity"            "Sales"               "Profits"            
## [10] "ShippingCost"
t4Africa <- dplyr::filter(M2Data, Market == "Africa")

africa_products <- t4Africa %>%
  count(`Product_Category`) %>%  
  arrange(desc(n))

pie_colors <- brewer.pal(n = nrow(africa_products), name = "Set3")

pie(africa_products$n,
    labels = paste(africa_products$`Product_Category`, "\n", 
                  africa_products$n, "units"),
    col = pie_colors,
    main = "Product Distribution in African Market")

legend("topright",
       legend = africa_products$`Product_Category`,
       fill = pie_colors,
       cex = 0.8)


Observations: The pie chart shows the distribution of different product categories in the African market. Technology products dominate with 30 units (55.6%), while Furniture displays for 13 units (24.1%) and Office Supplies represents 11 units (20.3%). This distribution suggests a strong preference for technology products in the African market, with Furniture and Office Supplies showing relatively similar but lower demand levels.

Task 8: Total Sales per Region in African Market
Description of task: This task calculates the total sales for each region in the African market using the tapply() function and presents the results using a bar plot with enhanced visualization features. 

totalSales <- tapply(t4Africa$Sales, t4Africa$Region, sum)

sales_df <- data.frame(
  Region = names(totalSales),
  Sales = as.numeric(totalSales)
)
sales_df <- sales_df[order(sales_df$Sales, decreasing = TRUE), ]

par(mar = c(7, 5, 4, 2))  

region_colors <- brewer.pal(n = length(totalSales), name = "Set3")

barplot_output <- barplot(sales_df$Sales,
        names.arg = sales_df$Region,
        col = region_colors,
        main = "Total Sales by Region in African Market",
        ylab = "Total Sales",
        las = 2,       
        cex.names = 0.8,
        ylim = c(0, max(sales_df$Sales) * 1.1))  

text(x = barplot_output,
     y = sales_df$Sales,
     labels = format(round(sales_df$Sales, 2), big.mark = ","),
     pos = 3, 
     cex = 0.8)

box()


Observations: 1. The bar plot shows the total sales distribution across different regions in the African market 2. Each region is represented by a distinct color for easy differentiation 3. The actual sales values are displayed on top of each bar for precise reference 4. We can clearly see which regions are generating the highest and lowest total sales 5. The visualization helps identify regional sales patterns and potential areas for market development

Task 10: Understanding R Data Types

Here are the key differences between the main data types in R:

Integer: - Represents whole numbers without decimal points - Uses less memory than double/numeric types - Examples: 1L, 2L, 3L (the ‘L’ suffix explicitly declares an integer) - Commonly used for counting and indexing (Kabacoff, 2022)

Factor: - Used for categorical variables with predefined levels - Stores data more efficiently than character strings - Essential for statistical modeling and plotting - Can be ordered (ordinal) or unordered (nominal) - Particularly useful in statistical analysis and data visualization (Kabacoff, 2022)

Double: - Represents decimal numbers with high precision - Default numeric type in R - Can handle very large or small numbers using scientific notation - Uses 64-bit floating-point representation (Chambers, 2023)

Numeric: - Generic term that includes both integer and double types - R automatically converts between integer and double as needed - Most mathematical operations return numeric type - Default choice for mathematical computations (Bluman, 2017)

Key differences in application:

  1. Memory usage: Integers use less memory than doubles
  2. Precision: Doubles offer more precision for decimal values
  3. Usage context: Factors are optimized for categorical data
  4. Computation speed: Integers are generally faster for basic operations


Task 11: Enhanced Profit Distribution Visualizations
Description of task: This task creates an improved presentation of profit distribution using both a boxplot and histogram, arranged in a 2x1 matrix layout with enhanced visual features. 

par(mfcol = c(2,1),     
    mai = c(1, 1, 0.2, 0.4), 
    mar = c(4,4,0.5,2))     

boxplot(M2Data$Profits,
        horizontal = TRUE,
        col = "lightblue",
        border = "steelblue",
        main = "",
        xlab = "Profit Amount",
        outCol = "red",        
        medCol = "darkblue")    

points(mean(M2Data$Profits), 1, 
       pch = 16,              
       col = "darkred",
       cex = 1.5)            

hist(M2Data$Profits,
     breaks = 50,
     col = "lightgreen",
     border = "darkgreen",
     main = "",
     xlab = "Profit Amount",
     ylab = "Frequency",
     las = 1)                 

abline(v = mean(M2Data$Profits), 
       col = "darkred", 
       lwd = 2, 
       lty = 2)             

legend("topright", 
       legend = paste("Mean =", round(mean(M2Data$Profits), 2)),
       col = "darkred", 
       lty = 2, 
       lwd = 2,
       cex = 0.8)


Observations: 1. The boxplot shows: - The distribution of profits - Outliers in red - The median as a dark blue line - The mean as a dark red point 2. The histogram reveals: - The frequency distribution of profits - A dashed red line indicating the mean - 50 breaks for detailed distribution view 3. Both plots are aligned vertically for easy comparison 4. The color scheme enhances readability and visual appeal


Task 12: Profit Analysis for Latin American Market
Description of task: This task analyzes the profit distribution specifically for the Latin American market using filtered data, presented through both a boxplot and histogram with enhanced visualizations. 

t13LATAM <- dplyr::filter(M2Data, Market == "LATAM")

par(mfcol = c(2,1),
    mai = c(1, 1, 0.2, 0.4),
    mar = c(4,4,0.5,2))

boxplot(t13LATAM$Profits,
        horizontal = TRUE,
        col = "lightsalmon",
        border = "coral3",
        main = "",
        xlab = "Profit Amount in Latin American Market",
        outCol = "red",
        medCol = "darkred")

points(mean(t13LATAM$Profits), 1,
       pch = 16,
       col = "darkblue",
       cex = 1.5)

legend("topright",
       legend = c("Mean", "Outliers"),
       col = c("darkblue", "red"),
       pch = c(16, 1),
       cex = 0.8)

hist(t13LATAM$Profits,
     breaks = 30,
     col = "lightblue",
     border = "steelblue",
     main = "",
     xlab = "Profit Amount in Latin American Market",
     ylab = "Frequency",
     las = 1)

abline(v = mean(t13LATAM$Profits),
       col = "darkblue",
       lwd = 2,
       lty = 2)

legend("topright",
       legend = paste("Mean =", round(mean(t13LATAM$Profits), 2)),
       col = "darkblue",
       lty = 2,
       lwd = 2,
       cex = 0.8)


Observations: 1. Boxplot Analysis: - Shows the central tendency and spread of profits in LATAM - Identifies potential outliers in the market - The mean (blue dot) relative to the median (red line) indicates the distribution’s skewness - The box width shows the interquartile range of profits

  1. Histogram Analysis:
    • Displays the frequency distribution of profits
    • The dashed blue line represents the mean profit
    • Shows the shape of the profit distribution (whether symmetric, skewed, or multimodal)
    • Reveals any unusual patterns or clusters in profit values
  2. Combined Insights:
    • Both visualizations complement each other to provide a comprehensive view of LATAM profit distribution
    • The histogram shows the detailed distribution while the boxplot summarizes key statistics
    • Together they help identify any unusual patterns or concerns in the LATAM market profits


Task 13: Total Sales per Region in Latin America
Description of task: This task calculates and presents the total sales for each region within the Latin American market using tapply() and creates a professionally formatted table using kable().

Task 14: Profit Distribution by Region in Latin American Market
Description of task: This task creates a side-by-side boxplot comparing profit distributions across different regions within the Latin American market, with enhanced labeling and presentation. 

par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))  

boxplot(Profits ~ Region, 
        data = t13LATAM,
        col = "lightgray",
        border = "darkgray",
        outCol = "black",
        medCol = "black",
        whiskcol = "black",
        staplewex = 0.5,
        outpch = 1,
        outcex = 0.8,
        main = "Profit Distribution by Region in Latin American Market",
        ylab = "Profit Amount ($)",
        xlab = "Geographic Region",
        cex.main = 1.2,   
        cex.lab = 1.1,     
        cex.axis = 0.9,    
        las = 1)           

grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, lty = 2, col = "gray80")

means <- tapply(t13LATAM$Profits, t13LATAM$Region, mean)
points(1:length(means), means, 
       pch = 16,          
       col = "darkred",
       cex = 1.2)

legend("topright", 
       legend = "Mean",
       pch = 16,
       col = "darkred",
       cex = 0.8,
       bg = "white")

box()


Observations: 1. The boxplot compares profit distributions across LATAM regions with: - Clear axis labels indicating measurement units - Horizontal y-axis labels for better readability - Mean values shown as red dots for each region - Grid lines to facilitate value comparison

  1. Distribution Features:
    • The boxes show the interquartile range (IQR)
    • The horizontal line in each box represents the median
    • Whiskers extend to the most extreme non-outlier values
    • Individual points represent outliers
    • Red dots indicate mean values for each region
  2. Visual Enhancements:
    • Professional grayscale color scheme
    • Appropriately sized labels and title
    • Added legend for mean indicators
    • Grid lines for easier value comparison
    • Clear border around the entire plot

CONCLUSIONS

This comprehensive analysis of global market performance has revealed several key insights and opportunities for strategic improvement. The investigation of sales patterns and profit distributions across different regions has highlighted both strengths and areas requiring attention in our global operations. I gained proficiency in implementing and interpreting various statistical graphs such as barplot, histogram, pie chart, and many more.

Key Strategic Findings:

  1. Regional Performance Variations
  • Profit margins vary greatly between regions
  • Success of product types changes from one market to another
  • Shipping costs affect profits differently in each region
  1. Market-Specific Insights
  • Africa shows growth potential despite current low presence
  • Latin American regions demonstrate diverse profit patterns requiring tailored approaches
  • How well product subtypes perform changes by region
  1. Operational Implications
  • Shipping cost optimization opportunities identified
  • How product types are spread out suggests chances for focused market growth
  • Differences in regional profits show need for strategies tailored to each market

Recommendations:

  1. Market Growth
  • Increase presence in African markets, focusing on products that sell well there
  • Set prices differently in each region based on profit analysis
  • Create specific marketing plans for regions with lower sales
  1. Operational Efficiency
  • Optimize shipping routes and methods based on regional cost analysis
  • Change product mix according to what sells well in each region
  • Manage inventory differently for each region
  1. Future Considerations
  • Keep track of how each region performs regularly
  • Continuous assessment of product category performance
  • Develop growth plans specific to each region
